sla_name: Singular and plural forms of objects found at home
sla_assessment_criteria: Pupil correctly points to and names one object and more than one of the same object found at home using pictures.
sla_teaching_aids: Pictures of objects found at home|Real objects from the classroom (chair, cup, plate)|Wall chart of home objects
sla_references: TET(2023), LEARN ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD TWO, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Introduces the idea that when we have one item we use its singular name, and when we have more than one we add letters to show more than one; grounded in the book's picture-based Activity 1 under 'I use singular and plural forms.'
sla_notes_details: Pupils look at pictures showing one object and pictures showing many of the same object, then say the name for one (singular) and the name for more than one (plural).
sla_notes_illustrations: One chair / many chairs, one spoon / many spoons, one cup / many cups (from the pictures of objects found at home).
sla_notes_daily_life: At home, a pupil can tell their mother 'There is one spoon' or 'There are many spoons' when helping to set the table.
sla_exercise: What do we call it when there is only one object?::Singular||What do we call it when there is more than one object?::Plural||Look at a picture of one cup and many cups. What are the two forms called?::One cup is singular, many cups is plural

specific_competence_name: Develop listening and speaking skills in different contexts
learning_activity_name: Use singular and plural forms of names of objects found in the immediate environment
sla_name: Plural forms of household objects using -s
sla_assessment_criteria: Pupil correctly adds -s to at least four singular household object names to form their plural.
sla_teaching_aids: Word cards for chair, spoon, cow, bed, jug, tree, axe, cup, plate, cat|Real classroom objects (chair, cup)|Word list chart
sla_references: TET(2023), LEARN ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD TWO, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Most singular nouns are made plural simply by adding the letter -s, as shown in the book's word pairs chair-chairs, spoon-spoons, cow-cows, bed-beds.
sla_notes_details: Pupils read the singular form, then add -s and pronounce the plural form for each household item.
sla_notes_illustrations: chair -> chairs, spoon -> spoons, cow -> cows, bed -> beds, jug -> jugs, tree -> trees, cup -> cups, plate -> plates, cat -> cats.
sla_notes_daily_life: A pupil counting cups at home can say 'one cup, two cups' when helping wash dishes.
sla_exercise: What is the plural of chair?::chairs||What is the plural of spoon?::spoons||What is the plural of cow?::cows||What is the plural of bed?::beds

sla_name: Plural forms with -es and -ies endings
sla_assessment_criteria: Pupil correctly forms the plural of words ending in -ch, -x, -sh with -es, and words ending in a consonant plus -y with -ies.
sla_teaching_aids: Word cards for match, box, dish, battery, puppy, berry|Pictures of matches, boxes, dishes, batteries, puppies, berries
sla_references: TET(2023), LEARN ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD TWO, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Some words need -es to form the plural (match-matches, box-boxes, dish-dishes) while words ending in a consonant and y change the y to i and add -es (battery-batteries, puppy-puppies, berry-berries).
sla_notes_details: Pupils read each singular-plural pair aloud and identify the pattern used to form the plural.
sla_notes_illustrations: match -> matches, box -> boxes, dish -> dishes, battery -> batteries, puppy -> puppies, berry -> berries.
sla_notes_daily_life: A pupil can ask for 'two boxes of chalk' or say 'three matches' when helping at home.
sla_exercise: What is the plural of match?::matches||What is the plural of box?::boxes||What is the plural of puppy?::puppies||What is the plural of berry?::berries

sla_notes_details: Pupils listen to a sentence with a gap and say it with the correct singular or plural form, e.g. 'I switch on the radio.' / 'I switch on the radios.'
sla_notes_illustrations: Turn on the fan. / Turn on the fans. We use a broom to sweep the floor. / We use brooms to sweep the floor. I like playing with a toy. / I like playing with toys.
sla_notes_daily_life: A pupil at home can correctly say 'Turn on the fans' when asked to switch on more than one fan.

sla_notes_details: The full stop tells a reader that a sentence has ended. Without it, a reader cannot tell where one sentence stops and the next one begins.

sla_notes_daily_life: I put a full stop after writing 'I did my homework.' in my diary at home.

sla_notes_intro: The book opens the topic with the fact that there are seven days in a week, then teaches the days through a song: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday and Sunday.
sla_notes_details: Pupils first learn the seven day names in fixed order through the song, then practise identifying 'today', and finally practise re-arranging a jumbled list of day names into the correct weekly order.
sla_notes_illustrations: Using the book's song 'There are seven days in a week. Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday and Sunday. Now I know the seven days of a week', pupils sing and point to each day on the calendar chart, then answer 'What day is it today?'
sla_notes_daily_life: Knowing the days of the week in order helps a pupil know when it is a school day and when it is a weekend.

sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil masters this SLA when he/she can ask and answer 'When does/do ... ?' questions about a weekly activity using the correct day of the week.
sla_teaching_aids: Days-and-activities table chart|Role-play cards for John and Asha dialogue|Calendar chart
sla_references: TET(2023), LEARN ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD TWO, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The book introduces day-linked activities through a dialogue between John and Asha about what they do every Monday, on Saturday and on Sunday, and through a table matching each day of the week to a class activity.
sla_notes_details: Pupils act out the John-Asha dialogue in pairs, then read a table of days and activities (Monday: pupils clean the classroom; Tuesday: Mpoki mops the floor; Wednesday: Musa waters the garden; Thursday: Stella sings a song; Friday: Frank sweeps the floor) and answer 'When does ... ?' questions about it, before saying what they themselves normally do on each day.
sla_notes_illustrations: In the dialogue, John says he usually does his homework and watches the news after school on Monday, and that on Saturday he will clean his room and play with friends while Asha will attend a music class. In the table, Mpoki mops the floor on Tuesday, Musa waters the garden on Wednesday, Stella sings a song on Thursday, and Frank sweeps the floor on Friday.
sla_notes_daily_life: A pupil uses these patterns to tell family members which day he/she does chores like sweeping, cleaning, or watering plants at home.

sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil masters this SLA when he/she can recite the twelve months of the year in order and state which month comes before or after a given month.
sla_teaching_aids: Calendar chart|Months-of-the-year song chart|Numbered months table
sla_references: TET(2023), LEARN ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD TWO, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The book opens the topic with the fact that there are twelve months in a year, then teaches the months through a song: January, February, March, April, May, June, July, August, September, October, November, and December.
sla_notes_details: After singing the months in order, pupils orally answer sequencing questions such as which month is last, which comes after March, and which comes before June; they then copy and complete a table matching numbers 1 to 12 with their correct month names.
sla_notes_illustrations: Using the book's song 'There are twelve months in the year... Now I know the twelve months of the year', pupils practise answers such as: the last month of the year is December; the month after March is April; the month between January and March is February; and they fill in the numbers table, e.g. number 1 is January, number 8 is December, number 7 is March.
sla_notes_daily_life: Knowing the months in order helps a pupil know how many months are left before their birthday or before the school year ends.
sla_exercise: How many months are there in a year?::There are twelve months in a year.||Which is the last month of the year?::December is the last month of the year.||Which month comes after March?::April comes after March.||Which month is between January and March?::February is between January and March.

sla_notes_intro: The book links each month to a real event or activity done by named people, such as John attending Workers' Day in May, and teaches pupils to answer 'When does ... ?' questions using the pattern 'in + month'.
sla_notes_details: Pupils read a table pairing each month of the year with a sentence about a named person or group's activity or celebration, study the worked example about John and Workers' Day, and then answer similar questions about the remaining eleven months.

sla_notes_daily_life: A pupil can use these patterns to tell others in which month his/her own birthday or a family celebration falls.
